title: Five Ways to Write It Up
scopeNote: This keeps the fixed ledger, the five accounts and the ledger entry that four of them have no place for. The original asks four questions of every account, twenty judgements in all; this asks one, the authority question, because it is the sharpest and because the other three read better together in the comparison than answered one at a time.
summary: Eight undisputed events and five accurate accounts of them. Each produces a different kind of person, makes a different next step obvious, entitles somebody different to speak, and four of the five have nowhere to put the decision that started it.
learningObjectives: Identify the subject position an account makes available.
Say which actions a position renders reasonable and which it removes.
Say who an account entitles to describe what is happening.
Recognise that what an account cannot say about anything other than the person is often the most consequential thing about it.
Distinguish analysing how something is written up from claiming that only the writing is real.
interactionTypes: a prediction about what sort of entry goes missing
five accounts opened one at a time
one judgement per account before its analysis is shown
a five-way comparison of position, next step, authority and omission
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Nothing is asked about the reader.
dataStatus: R, the service and all five accounts are invented. No real person, record, organisation or document is described.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The account is a group of native radio buttons in a labelled fieldset, and the authority question is a choice grid whose options carry three non-colour state signals plus a visually hidden sentence naming the state; once answered, every option is locked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute so it stays reachable and readable, and each names the account it is the right answer for. The ledger is a numbered list that stays on screen throughout. The comparison is a real table with row and column headers and its final column is given in words. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: Every account is compatible with the whole ledger and none is marked true or false. Two design decisions carry the critical content and both are preserved from the original. The ledger stays on screen, which is the guard against reading discourse analysis as a claim that the events are made of language, and the test suite checks that it is byte-identical after every account has been opened. And the halving of the hours, which happened in April before anything R did, appears in one account of five; it is the only entry in the ledger about a decision rather than about a person, and an account written about a person has nowhere to put it. The commissioning report comes closest of the other four and has the hours only as a model implemented on schedule, which is not the same entry. The five authority options are each the correct answer for exactly one account, so a wrong answer is a right answer about a different account and the feedback says which; unchosen options name the account they belong to as well. This is not a ranking: the case note and the risk register exist for reasons a page that could not note declining attendance or an unassessed setting would be worse for lacking, the recovery vocabulary was fought for by service users against exactly the case-note position, and the advocacy bulletin is not neutral either.
readmeTopic: how an accurate account decides what kind of person somebody is and what happens next
